notes.meaning: In the third year of King Cyrus, around 536 BC, God gave an aged Daniel one last message. He gives his Babylonian name, Belteshazzar, so readers know he is the same Daniel carried off to Babylon long before. He says the message is true and can be trusted. It is about a great conflict, meaning hard times and wars for God's people. This time Daniel was helped to understand what he was shown.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars think chapters 10–12 were written after the events they describe, in the second century BC. Daniel 11 is so detailed that they treat it as history, not prediction.

notes.meaning: For three full weeks Daniel mourned and fasted. He gave up fine food, meat and wine, and he did not use oil on his skin, which was a sign of joy. He was grieving over his people. Only a few had gone home, and enemies were blocking the rebuilding of the temple. His fasting was a sign of sorrow and a help to prayer, not a way to earn God's favor.

The vision came on the 24th day of the first month, called Nisan. This was the month of Passover, when Israel remembered being set free from Egypt. That made it a fitting time to grieve over their troubles. Daniel was really standing beside the Tigris River with some companions.

Daniel looked up and saw a glorious man dressed in linen, wearing a belt of fine gold. His body shone like a precious stone. His face flashed like lightning, his eyes blazed like torches, and his voice roared like a crowd. Many traditional commentators believe this is the Son of God before he was born as a man. John saw him looking much the same in Revelation 1:13–15.

differ.view: This is a great angel in human form, sent from heaven. The details are meant to show he is no ordinary man, not to picture Christ's priesthood.

notes.meaning: Only Daniel saw the vision. The men with him saw nothing, but they were struck with terror and ran to hide. It is like Paul's companions on the road to Damascus, who sensed something without seeing Christ. Their fear shows the vision was real, not something Daniel imagined.

Left alone, Daniel lost all his strength and turned deathly pale. Even the best people cannot bear a direct sight of God's glory. God humbles us like this so that our pride gives way and we are ready to listen.
When Daniel heard the man's voice, he fell face down and fainted, as if in a deep sleep. Lying face down is also the posture of humble worship.

A hand touched Daniel and raised him, trembling, onto his hands and knees. Many older commentators think it was the hand of the angel Gabriel. When God's greatness knocks us down, only his hand, meaning his power, can lift us up. Strength often comes back a little at a time.

The messenger called Daniel a man highly precious, deeply loved by God. He told him to listen carefully and stand up, because he had been sent to him. Daniel stood, but he was still trembling. God often restores us step by step, not all at once.

"Do not be afraid," the messenger said. Daniel's prayer had been heard on the very first day he set his heart to understand and humbled himself before God. The messenger came because of those prayers. God hears prayer at once, even when the answer seems slow to arrive.

The messenger explains the delay. The "prince of Persia," an evil spiritual power standing behind the Persian kingdom, held him back for 21 days. That was the same length as Daniel's fast. Then Michael came to help. His name means "Who is like God?" and he is one of the highest angels, the protector of Israel. The verse pulls back the curtain on unseen battles behind world events.

differ.view: The "prince of Persia" was the Persian king Cambyses, who blocked the building of the temple. God's angel worked against him to stop him harming the Jews even more.
Michael is not a created angel but Christ himself, the head of the angels.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some teach that certain evil spirits rule over places, and that believers should pray against them by name to break their hold. Others answer that Daniel did not even know about this battle.

notes.meaning: The messenger came to show Daniel what would happen to his people in the latter days. The vision reaches far into the future. Much of it came true in the time of the cruel Greek king Antiochus, about 300 years later. It also points ahead to the coming of the Messiah.

differ.view: "The latter days" point mainly to the future of the nation of Israel at the end of this age, before Christ returns. The church does not replace Israel in this promise.

notes.meaning: While the messenger was speaking, Daniel bowed his face to the ground and could not speak. He was overcome with awe and deep reverence.

Someone who looked like a man touched Daniel's lips, and he could speak again. He said the vision had left him in anguish, like a woman's pains in childbirth. He felt he had no strength or breath. "My lord" is simply a polite title. Like Isaiah, Daniel felt the huge distance between weak people and the holy God.
The one who looked like a man touched Daniel again and gave him strength. Daniel needed a second touch. When God lifts up his children, he often does it little by little.

"Do not be afraid, you who are highly precious. Peace be with you! Be strong!" "Peace" meant God was kind toward Daniel and his people. Nothing lifts a downcast believer like being sure of God's love. When God says "be strong," his power comes with the word. Now Daniel was ready to listen.

The messenger asks a question to make Daniel stop and think. He must soon go back to fight the prince of Persia. After that, the prince of Greece will come. This points to the Greek empire founded by Alexander the Great, which would follow Persia. God's people face one enemy after another, but God keeps watch over them.

differ.view: The fight is against the human kings of Persia. God would hold back their cruelty, and later Alexander's, to protect his people.

notes.meaning: First the messenger will tell Daniel what is written in the Book of Truth. That means God's sure plan, which will certainly happen. No one stands with him against these enemies except Michael, the prince who protects Daniel's whole people. We should not expect much help from the world, but God's plan will stand.

differ.view: "Michael your prince" is Christ, the true protector and head of his people.
